name: Elections
description: Elections are taking place in Berland. There are $$$n$$$ candidates participating in the elections, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. The $$$i$$$-th candidate has $$$a_i$$$ fans who will vote for him. Additionally, there are $$$c$$$ people who are undecided about their favorite candidate, let's call them undecided . Undecided people will vote for the candidate with the lowest number. The candidate who receives the maximum number of votes wins the elections, and if multiple candidates receive the same maximum number of votes, the candidate with the lowest number among them wins. You found these elections too boring and predictable, so you decided to exclude some candidates from them. If you do not allow candidate number $$$i$$$ to participate in the elections, all $$$a_i$$$ of his fans will become undecided, and will vote for the candidate with the lowest number. You are curious to find, for each $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, the minimum number of candidates that need to be excluded from the elections for candidate number $$$i$$$ to win the elections.
input_specification: Each test consists of multiple test cases. The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 2 \cdot 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$c$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$0 \le c \le 10^9$$$) — the number of candidates in the elections and the number of undecided people. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$0 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$) — the number of fans for each candidate. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output $$$n$$$ integers, the $$$i$$$-th of which should be equal to the minimum number of candidates that need to be excluded from the elections for candidate number $$$i$$$ to win.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1978D — Elections [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
